cards.definition: Without or absence of. Asymptomatic means without symptoms.
Above normal or excessive. Hypertension is raised blood pressure.
Below normal or deficient. Hypoglycaemia is low blood glucose.
Fast. Tachycardia is a heart rate above 100 per minute.
Slow. Bradycardia is a heart rate below 60 per minute.
Difficult, painful or disordered. Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing.
Inflammation. Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining.
Surgical removal of. Appendicectomy is removal of the appendix.
Cutting into. Laparotomy is a surgical incision into the abdomen.
Creating a permanent opening. Colostomy brings colon to the skin.
Pain. Arthralgia is joint pain without swelling.
A condition of the blood. Anaemia is a low haemoglobin concentration.
A condition of the urine. Haematuria is blood in the urine.
Enlargement. Hepatomegaly is an enlarged liver.
A swelling or tumour. Lipoma is a benign fatty tumour.
Disease of. Neuropathy is disease of peripheral nerves.
Paralysis. Hemiplegia is paralysis of one side of the body.
Looking inside with an instrument. Endoscopy examines the gut lumen.
Recording or imaging. Radiography produces an X-ray image.
Heart. Cardiomegaly is an enlarged heart.

level2.name: The body: position, planes and regions

cards.definition: Standing upright, face forward, palms forward, feet together. Every direction is described from this reference.
A vertical plane dividing the body into left and right. The midline one is the median plane.
A vertical plane dividing the body into front and back.
A horizontal plane dividing the body into upper and lower parts.
Closer to the trunk or the point of origin.
Further from the trunk or the point of origin.
Medial is towards the midline, lateral is away from it.
Superior is towards the head, inferior is towards the feet.
Superficial is nearer the skin, deep is further from it.
Flexion decreases the angle at a joint, extension increases it.
Abduction moves a limb away from the midline, adduction brings it back.
Pronation turns the palm down, supination turns it up.
The space bounded by the ribs and diaphragm, holding heart, lungs and mediastinum.
The space from the diaphragm to the pelvic floor, holding gut, liver and pelvic organs.
Behind the peritoneal lining: kidneys, ureters, pancreas and great vessels lie here.
The upper central abdominal region, over the stomach and liver edge.
The lower right abdominal region, where the appendix and caecum sit.
The strip of skin supplied by one spinal nerve root.
One motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it supplies.
A connection between two vessels or tubes, natural or surgical.
Increase in cell size, giving a larger organ with the same number of cells.
Increase in cell number, usually in response to a stimulus.
One mature cell type is replaced by another, often a response to irritation.
Disordered growth with abnormal cells, a precursor of malignancy.
Programmed cell death, tidy and without inflammation.
Cell death from injury, with inflammation and loss of tissue architecture.
Ischaemic necrosis of tissue after loss of its blood supply.
Reduced blood flow to a tissue, which may be reversible.
Excess fluid in the interstitial space, producing swelling.
Exudate is protein rich and inflammatory, transudate is protein poor from pressure imbalance.
A collection of macrophages and giant cells walling off a persistent agent.
A thrombus forms in place, an embolus travels and lodges elsewhere.
Benign tumours stay local and well differentiated, malignant ones invade and metastasise.
Spread of malignant cells to a distant site through blood, lymph or seeding.
Malignant cells confined by the basement membrane, not yet invasive.
Haemoglobin below the reference range for age and sex.
A raised white cell count, often a response to infection.
Growing an organism and testing which antibiotics inhibit it.
Sensitivity finds the diseased, specificity excludes the healthy. Neither alone gives the probability of disease.
Idiopathic means no identifiable cause, iatrogenic means caused by medical care.
A symptom is what the patient reports, a sign is what the examiner finds.
Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associations, Timing, Exacerbating factors, Severity.
Breathlessness perceived by the patient.
Breathlessness on lying flat, counted in pillows.
Waking at night gasping, relieved by sitting up, typical of heart failure.
Transient loss of consciousness from cerebral hypoperfusion, with full recovery.
A false sense of movement, rotatory or swaying.
Muscle pain on walking that resolves with rest, from arterial insufficiency.
Coughing up blood from the respiratory tract.
Vomiting blood, usually from the upper gastrointestinal tract.
Black tarry stool from digested blood.
Waking at night to pass urine.
A painful urge to defecate with little or nothing passed.
Loss of the sense of smell.
Light causes discomfort, common in meningitis and migraine.
Involuntary abdominal wall tension, rigidity being the board-like extreme.
Pain worse on releasing pressure, suggesting peritoneal irritation.
A sound from turbulent blood flow across a valve or shunt.
Crackling breath sounds from collapsed or fluid-filled alveoli.
Fluid collecting in the feet and ankles, pitting on pressure.
Haemoglobin, white cells and platelets, the first line haematology screen.
Renal function and the common electrolytes, sodium and potassium.
Bilirubin, transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and albumin.
Acute phase markers of inflammation, neither is specific to one disease.
Cardiac protein released on myocyte injury, the marker for acute coronary syndrome.
Glycated haemoglobin reflecting average glucose over about three months.
Standardised prothrombin time used to dose warfarin and assess clotting.
Paired aerobic and anaerobic bottles taken before antibiotics in suspected sepsis.
pH, carbon dioxide, oxygen and bicarbonate, showing ventilation and acid base state.
A twelve lead recording of cardiac electrical activity, showing rhythm and ischaemia.
Ultrasound of the heart showing valves, chambers and ejection fraction.
Cross sectional imaging that shows acute bleeding, infarction and masses.
Magnetic resonance imaging, best for soft tissue, cord and brain.
Safe, real time imaging used for abdomen, vessels and obstetrics.
A camera passed into the gut lumen for direct view and biopsy.
A tissue sample examined histologically to give a definitive diagnosis.
CSF sampling from the lumbar subarachnoid space after excluding raised pressure.
A line into a large vein for drugs, fluids and central pressure measurement.
Drainage of the bladder, monitoring output and relieving retention.
Explaining indication, alternatives, risks and benefits before a procedure.

level3.name: Emergencies, safety and evidence

cards.definition: Oxygen, cultures, antibiotics, fluids, lactate and urine output within one hour.
Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure, treating each before moving on.
A track and trigger score from observations that flags a deteriorating patient.
A feature that raises the probability of serious disease and demands urgent action.
A condition where delay to treatment directly worsens outcome, such as stroke or sepsis.
A recorded decision that CPR would not succeed, made with the patient where possible.
The ability to understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision at that moment.
How many patients must be treated for one to benefit.
The chance a positive test is truly positive, which depends on prevalence.
Participants allocated by chance to intervention or control, the strongest design for causation.
Keeping allocation hidden from patient, clinician or assessor to reduce bias.
The range of values likely to contain the true effect, showing precision.
Audit checks practice against a standard, research creates new generalisable knowledge.
A ranked list of plausible diagnoses kept open until evidence narrows it.
Clear advice on what to watch for and when to return if things change.
Many medicines taken together, raising interaction and adverse effect risk.
Planned withdrawal of medicines that no longer give benefit.
Doctors, nurses, pharmacists and therapists planning care together.
Sorting patients by urgency so the sickest are seen first.
Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation, a structured clinical handover.
